synopsis: After Columbia's January 2003 foam strike, engineers used Crater, an empirical impact-penetration model, to assess tile damage; Columbia was lost on re-entry on 1 February 2003 [f7950, f15843, f14933]. The strike debris was about 400 times the size represented in Crater's test database, while an early briefing reported 640 times; in August 2003, the investigation board found that the assessment was well outside that database and that the analyst was inexperienced [f7582, f7951, f7952]. Crater had overpredicted penetration in small-impact calibration data, but engineers assumed that conservative bias would persist for the much larger strike and overrode its prediction of penetration deeper than the tile [f7955, f7956, f15845]. Chapter 10 presents this as a canonical false-confidence case illustrating the danger of extrapolation [f7581]. The booklet also records a dissenting interpretation: in a 2011 account, Wayne Hale argued that Crater correctly warned of unsafe damage and that management's override, rather than the model's warning, was the failure [f7960, f15853].
